curriculum.title: Soccer → machine learning

data.title: StatsBomb Open Data
data.use: Use the README, competition list, match files, event schema, and attribution terms. Select a historical competition with enough matches.

isl.title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning · Python
isl.use: Use selected chapters and Python labs. The book PDF is free on the authors’ site.

math.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
math.use: Use selected sections as a reference after the visual experiment. The authors provide a free PDF.

visual.title: 3Blue1Brown · visual mathematics
visual.use: Find the linear algebra and calculus lessons. Recreate one visual idea in code.

d2l.title: Dive into Deep Learning
d2l.use: Use the interactive book for calculus, automatic differentiation, training loops, and attention.

tabpfn.title: Accurate predictions on small data with a tabular foundation model · 2025
tabpfn.use: Read the question, evaluation design, and limitations. Reproduce one feasible comparison, not the original training run.

paper2026.title: Why Large Language Models Fail at Tabular Prediction · August 2026
paper2026.use: Treat this preprint as a claim to examine. Compare its evaluation choices with your soccer experiments. No paid API experiment is required.

research.title: Anthropic research
research.use: Select a recent public article about evaluations or model behavior. Follow its paper or methods link and record limitations.

careers.title: Anthropic careers
careers.use: Compare your evidence with a current engineering role. Requirements change. This curriculum does not guarantee a role or a credential.

modules.title: Start with a forecast
modules.question: Can a simple rule predict a match?
modules.outcome: Build a reproducible match table and a baseline: a simple reference prediction.
modules.math: Refresh fractions, ratios, percentages, means, variables, functions, and summation through match statistics.
tasks: Load historical matches. Record the source, download date, license, and a small data dictionary.
Create chronological training, validation, and untouched test sets. Count missing and duplicate rows.
Predict home/draw/away using training-set frequencies. Compute accuracy and Brier score, the squared error of probabilities.
Explain why a post-match statistic leaks the answer into a pre-match forecast. Record your baseline and evidence.
weeks: Week 1: Spend 6 h on data and code, 3 h on algebra through match summaries, and 2 h on a data audit.
Week 2: Spend 6 h on baselines, 3 h on probability arithmetic, and 2 h on evaluation and reflection.
modules.evidence: A runnable baseline, a data dictionary, split dates, and a one-page explanation of what the model knows before kickoff.
modules.challenge: Recompute a three-outcome Brier score for one match. Explain why all three probabilities must sum to one.
modules.reading: ISL chapter 2. Use a small competition first. Preserve the same held-out test period throughout the project.
modules.dataset: StatsBomb Open Data: competitions.json → matches/{competition_id}/{season_id}.json. Use scores, dates, and information available before kickoff. Build recent-form features only from earlier matches.

modules.title: Make the mathematics visible
modules.question: How do numbers become a model?
modules.outcome: Build a small interactive forecast with adjustable weights for recent form and home advantage.
modules.math: Refresh equations, slopes, powers, exponentials, logarithms, function composition, and coordinate plots.
tasks: Plot a weighted score as you vary each input. Label the units and ranges.
Convert scores to three probabilities with softmax, a function that turns scores into normalized probabilities.
Plot squared error and log loss as predictions become confidently wrong. Recreate one calculation without a model library.
Write what each symbol means and translate the formula into a small Python function.
weeks: Week 3: 6 h building the forecast, 3 h on functions and plots, 2 h explaining your outputs.
Week 4: 6 h exploring losses, 3 h on powers and logarithms, 2 h recording counterexamples.
modules.evidence: A notebook with adjustable inputs, labeled plots, and examples of confident errors.
modules.challenge: Explain why a tiny probability for the actual outcome produces a large log loss. Calculate one example.
modules.reading: ISL chapters 2 and 4. Use logarithms as measurements of multiplicative change.
modules.dataset: StatsBomb Open Data: competitions.json → matches/{competition_id}/{season_id}.json. Use scores, dates, and information available before kickoff. Build recent-form features only from earlier matches.

modules.title: Think in vectors
modules.question: Can a whole season be one calculation?
modules.outcome: Implement batched predictions with NumPy and build a player similarity explorer.
modules.math: Learn vectors, matrix shapes, dot products, norms, projections, rank, and feature scaling.
tasks: Represent matches as rows and pre-match measurements as columns. Annotate every matrix shape.
Compute one prediction with a loop and with a matrix product. Make sure that the results agree.
Build a player similarity search with normalized vectors. Show how scaling changes the neighbors.
Demonstrate redundant columns and explain why they create estimation problems.
weeks: Week 5: 6 h building vectorized forecasts, 3 h on vectors and shapes, 2 h explaining one example.
Week 6: 6 h on player similarity, 3 h on projections and rank, 2 h testing scaling choices.
modules.evidence: A matrix implementation with numerical comparisons and a similarity example whose behavior you can explain.
modules.challenge: Calculate a small dot product yourself. Diagnose a shape error and explain one misleading similarity result.
modules.reading: Mathematics for Machine Learning chapters 2 and 3. Read only the sections used by the experiments.
modules.dataset: StatsBomb Open Data: competitions.json → matches/{competition_id}/{season_id}.json. Use scores, dates, and information available before kickoff. Build recent-form features only from earlier matches. Player similarity uses player statistics aggregated from event files; restrict these to training matches.

modules.title: Learn from error
modules.question: How does a model learn its weights?
modules.outcome: Fit a linear model from scratch and compare it with a library implementation.
modules.math: Learn limits through finite differences, derivatives, partial derivatives, gradients, and the chain rule.
tasks: Plot an error curve. Estimate its slope with small input changes before using a derivative formula.
Derive the squared-error gradient for a linear model and implement gradient descent.
Compare analytic gradients with finite differences. Try several learning rates and explain divergence.
Fit a reference library model and compare predictions, training curves, and numerical stability.
weeks: Week 7: 6 h visualizing optimization, 3 h on derivatives, 2 h on numerical experiments.
Week 8: 6 h implementing training, 3 h on partial derivatives and the chain rule, 2 h explaining failures.
modules.evidence: A working training loop, gradient comparison, learning curves, and a written explanation of a failed learning rate.
modules.challenge: Derive one weight update, compute it on a tiny example, and explain how the loss changes.
modules.reading: Mathematics for Machine Learning chapters 5 and 7. D2L calculus and linear regression sections.
modules.dataset: StatsBomb Open Data: competitions.json → matches/{competition_id}/{season_id}.json. Use scores, dates, and information available before kickoff. Build recent-form features only from earlier matches.

modules.title: Predict goals and uncertainty
modules.question: What does a forecast actually promise?
modules.outcome: Build a Poisson goal model and simulate scorelines and season outcomes.
modules.math: Learn random variables, conditional probability, independence, expectation, variance, likelihood, and numerical integration.
tasks: Estimate goal rates using training data and plot a Poisson distribution, a model for event counts.
Simulate scorelines and derive home/draw/away probabilities. Account for truncated probability mass.
Compare forecasts with the baseline. Explain when independent goal counts are a poor assumption.
Resample matches to estimate uncertainty. Distinguish outcome uncertainty from uncertainty in estimated performance.
weeks: Week 9: 6 h on goal models, 3 h on probability and likelihood, 2 h on simulation.
Week 10: 6 h on uncertainty experiments, 3 h on expectations and numerical sums, 2 h on a model critique.
modules.evidence: A goal model, a scoreline simulator, and an evaluation with uncertainty and stated assumptions.
modules.challenge: Explain why a 70% forecast can lose. Calculate conditional probability on a small match table.
modules.reading: Mathematics for Machine Learning chapter 6. Use simulation before formal probability notation.
modules.dataset: StatsBomb Open Data: competitions.json → matches/{competition_id}/{season_id}.json. Use scores, dates, and information available before kickoff. Build recent-form features only from earlier matches.

modules.title: Build expected goals
modules.question: Which shots turn into goals?
modules.outcome: Train logistic regression to estimate expected goals: the scoring probability of a shot.
modules.math: Learn distance and angle geometry, sigmoid, log likelihood, regularization, and probability calibration.
tasks: Extract shots and outcomes. Compute distance and angle to goal from pitch coordinates.
Split by match and date so shots from one match cannot cross partitions. Fit preprocessing on training data only.
Implement a small logistic model and compare it with a library model. Tune regularization on validation data.
Compare log loss and Brier score with a constant baseline. Plot calibration, the agreement between predicted and observed frequencies.
weeks: Week 11: 6 h on shot data, 3 h on geometry and sigmoid, 2 h on split design.
Week 12: 6 h on logistic models, 3 h on likelihood and regularization, 2 h on calibration.
modules.evidence: An expected-goals model with grouped chronological splits, calibration plots, and a baseline comparison.
modules.challenge: Explain why shot outcome is a target and provider expected-goals values are excluded from your input features.
modules.reading: ISL chapters 4 and 6. Keep vendor expected-goals estimates out of the training features.
modules.dataset: StatsBomb Open Data: events/{match_id}.json joined to match dates. For shots, use shot locations and outcomes. Split by whole match and date.

modules.title: Run fair comparisons
modules.question: Does complexity earn its place?
modules.outcome: Compare trees and boosting with your linear and logistic models.
modules.math: Learn bias and variance, resampling, generalization, and regularization through model comparisons.
tasks: Train a decision tree and a boosted tree model on the same task and partitions.
Run a small declared parameter search with chronological validation folds. Keep preprocessing inside each fold.
Record at least three controlled experiments. Change one design choice in each experiment.
Compare quality, runtime, and stability. Explain an overfit model and one result that contradicts your expectation.
weeks: Week 13: 6 h on trees and boosting, 3 h on bias and variance, 2 h designing comparisons.
Week 14: 6 h running experiments, 3 h on resampling, 2 h writing a result table.
modules.evidence: A reproducible comparison of at least three model families and three experiments with explicit hypotheses.
modules.challenge: Explain why selecting a model using test scores invalidates the final test. Repair a deliberately flawed evaluation.
modules.reading: ISL chapters 5, 6, and 8. Prefer small searches with clear questions over large parameter sweeps.
modules.dataset: StatsBomb Open Data: events/{match_id}.json joined to match dates. For shots, use shot locations and outcomes. Split by whole match and date.

modules.title: Build a neural network
modules.question: Can learned features improve the forecast?
modules.outcome: Train a small PyTorch network for the shot prediction task.
modules.math: Apply the chain rule to backpropagation, the calculation of gradients through a network.
tasks: Implement a two-layer network and annotate tensor shapes. Compare a tiny manual gradient with automatic differentiation.
Write a training loop with batches, validation, reproducible seeds, and saved model weights.
Overfit a tiny batch to diagnose the pipeline. Then use early stopping on the real training split.
Compare the network with logistic regression and boosting. Report when the neural network loses.
weeks: Week 15: 6 h implementing the network, 3 h on the chain rule, 2 h explaining gradients.
Week 16: 6 h on training and diagnostics, 3 h on optimization, 2 h on the comparison.
modules.evidence: A reproducible neural training run, a tiny-batch diagnostic, learning curves, and comparisons with simpler models.
modules.challenge: Trace a prediction and gradient through a tiny network. Explain train versus evaluation mode.
modules.reading: D2L chapters on linear networks, multilayer perceptrons, and training. Keep the network small enough for local experiments.
modules.dataset: StatsBomb Open Data: events/{match_id}.json joined to match dates. For shots, use shot locations and outcomes. Split by whole match and date.

modules.title: Understand attention
modules.question: Can the order of events help prediction?
modules.outcome: Build a small sequence model and an attention calculation for soccer events.
modules.math: Learn embeddings, softmax attention, positional information, and masking through matrix operations.
tasks: Define a next-event task with information available at prediction time. Split by match and date.
Build a frequency baseline and a small recurrent or pooled-embedding baseline.
Implement scaled dot-product attention on a tiny sequence. Demonstrate why a future-event mask matters.
Train a small attention model if time permits. Otherwise evaluate the simpler sequence model and document the attention prototype.
weeks: Week 17: 6 h on sequence data and a baseline, 3 h on embeddings, 2 h testing chronology.
Week 18: 6 h on attention, 3 h on matrix operations and masks, 2 h on evidence.
modules.evidence: A sequence baseline, a correct attention demonstration, and a clear account of whether training improved the task.
modules.challenge: Explain how attention weights are calculated and show a future-information leak prevented by a mask.
modules.reading: D2L attention and transformer chapters. Full transformer training is a stretch goal, not a completion requirement.
modules.dataset: StatsBomb events/{match_id}.json: ordered events within each match. Define the target at a fixed prediction time and exclude all later events.

modules.title: Read research like an engineer
modules.question: Which claims survive a closer look?
modules.outcome: Write two structured paper notes and design a small reproduction.
modules.math: Connect assumptions, objective functions, experimental controls, effect sizes, and uncertainty to research claims.
tasks: Read the 2025 TabPFN paper and the 2026 tabular-prediction preprint. Record question, method, evidence, and limitations.
Trace one central equation into pseudocode. List every concept you cannot yet explain.
Choose one feasible claim about evaluation or tabular prediction. Specify data, baseline, metric, compute budget, and failure criteria.
Read one current Anthropic evaluation article. Explain how its evaluation principles transfer to your experiments.
weeks: Week 19: 6 h reading and annotating two papers, 3 h unpacking notation, 2 h writing critiques.
Week 20: 6 h designing a reproduction, 3 h studying missing concepts, 2 h selecting a current evaluation article.
modules.evidence: Two paper notes, one current research note, and a preregistered reproduction plan with a local compute budget.
modules.challenge: Separate an author claim from evidence and your inference. Name a confounder that can reverse the conclusion.
modules.reading: Use abstracts to choose questions, then inspect methods and limitations. Refresh the current article when this stage begins.
modules.dataset: Reuse the frozen soccer datasets and splits. For reproduction, use the selected paper’s public data if feasible; otherwise label the soccer experiment as an adaptation.

modules.title: Reproduce and investigate
modules.question: Can you recover a result and explain a failure?
modules.outcome: Reproduce one limited research result and run an ablation, an experiment that removes one component.
modules.math: Apply confidence intervals, seed variability, multiple-comparison caution, and controlled comparisons.
tasks: Freeze data and code versions. Implement the selected experiment with a baseline and an explicit compute limit.
Run multiple seeds or resamples where appropriate. Record metrics and variation, not only the best run.
Remove one component and compare the result. Investigate a discrepancy with the original claim.
Write a short report that distinguishes exact reproduction, adaptation, and failure to reproduce.
weeks: Week 21: 6 h implementing the reproduction, 3 h on uncertainty, 2 h recording the protocol.
Week 22: 6 h on ablations, 3 h analyzing discrepancies, 2 h writing the report.
modules.evidence: A rerunnable experiment, an ablation table, and a report with limitations and negative results.
modules.challenge: Explain which conclusion your data supports and which it does not. Rerun one result from a clean command.
modules.reading: If pretrained weights or hardware are unavailable, reproduce an evaluation comparison using your existing models and label the adaptation.
modules.dataset: Reuse the frozen soccer datasets and splits. For reproduction, use the selected paper’s public data if feasible; otherwise label the soccer experiment as an adaptation.

modules.title: Turn a model into a system
modules.question: Can another engineer trust and run your model?
modules.outcome: Package a local prediction service and an evaluation harness, code that measures model behavior consistently.
modules.math: Study numerical stability, data contracts, profiling, test design, and distribution shift through your own system.
tasks: Package preprocessing and model weights together. Add a command that reproduces evaluation from saved data.
Test malformed inputs, missing values, changed categories, and data from a later period.
Measure prediction latency and memory use. Compare single predictions with batches. Document environment and model provenance.
Create a model report with intended use, training data, limitations, calibration, and monitoring signals.
weeks: Week 23: 6 h packaging and tests, 3 h on numerical and data failures, 2 h documenting the run command.
Week 24: 6 h on profiling and evaluation, 3 h on drift, 2 h writing the model report.
modules.evidence: A local service or CLI, an evaluation harness, failure tests, performance measurements, and clear run instructions.
modules.challenge: Debug a failing prediction without an AI agent writing the fix. Explain how you would detect changing input data.
modules.reading: Use existing software skills. Spend time on ML-specific failure modes rather than introductory web development.
modules.dataset: Reuse the frozen soccer datasets and splits. For reproduction, use the selected paper’s public data if feasible; otherwise label the soccer experiment as an adaptation.

modules.title: Make the work legible
modules.question: What can you now demonstrate independently?
modules.outcome: Finish two portfolio projects and assess the next six months against actual roles.
modules.math: Integrate mathematical explanations, experimental reasoning, and engineering tradeoffs.
tasks: Finish a soccer prediction project with multiple models and a separate research reproduction with an ablation.
Give a recorded walkthrough: problem, data, loss, split, baseline, result, limitation, and next experiment.
Complete an independent exercise: train a simple model, explain its gradients, and diagnose a leaked feature.
Compare your evidence with two current engineering roles. Record gaps and select the next six-month focus.
weeks: Week 25: 6 h finishing projects, 3 h revisiting weak mathematics, 2 h on a technical walkthrough.
Week 26: 6 h on independent assessment, 3 h on role analysis, 2 h planning the next phase.
modules.evidence: Two polished repositories or local project bundles, a technical walkthrough, and an honest skills assessment with a follow-on plan.
modules.challenge: Explain and modify your core model without generated code. Defend the experimental design and describe a result you do not trust.
modules.reading: The target is a stronger ML engineering portfolio. Frontier-lab hiring is selective and is not a guaranteed outcome of 286 study hours.
modules.dataset: Reuse the frozen soccer datasets and splits. For reproduction, use the selected paper’s public data if feasible; otherwise label the soccer experiment as an adaptation.

nextPhase: Deeper probability, Bayesian inference, optimization, and proof-based reasoning.
Large-scale training, distributed systems, GPU programming, and performance engineering.
Language-model training and evaluation, interpretability, and a sustained open-source contribution.
A larger research reproduction with mentorship and role-specific interview practice.
curriculum.subtitle: YOUR NEXT SIX MONTHS
curriculum.description: Build soccer models. Learn the mathematics. Run experiments that you can explain.

m01.notes: Synthetic note: split the matches by date before any model.
